Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Explain the etiology and pathoanatomy of Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease.
Review treatment recommendations and outcomes based on the age of onset of Legg-Calvé-
Perthes disease and the severity of the disease process.
Describe symptoms and treatment recommendations for adolescents and young adults with
symptoms related to residual deformity after Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Current theories propose that a disruption of the vascularity of the proximal femoral epiphysis
is the key pathogenic event in Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease (LCPD), resulting in ischemic
necrosis, epiphyseal fragmentation, and subsequent revascularization.1

The abnormal femoral head (weakened by ischemia) can deform if its mechanical strength is
surpassed by loading forces on the hip joint. This deformity may eventually remodel with
healing and revascularization; however, the shape of the femoral head at final healing
depends on the extent of its containment within the acetabulum.
The articular cartilage, capital epiphysis, physis, and metaphysis of the hip joint are
histologically abnormal in patients with LCPD, with disorganized cartilaginous areas of
hypercellularity and fibrillation.
Overview
LCPD is an idiopathic osteonecrosis of the femoral head that occurs in children, typically with
onset between ages 4 to 8 years.
Involvement can include the capital femoral epiphysis, physis, and the proximal femoral
metaphysis, depending on severity.
Outcomes vary based on the age at onset and the severity of involvement, ultimately
correlating with sphericity of the femoral head after re-ossification and remodeling at skeletal
maturity.
Treatment goals include preservation of hip motion and containment of the femoral head
within the acetabulum during disease progression because improved containment may result
in maintained sphericity, subsequent joint congruency, and improved long-term outcome.
Epidemiology
LCPD affects 1 in 1,200 children.
It affects boys four to five times more than girls.
Bilateral hip involvement is present in 10% to 15% of patients. If both hips are in the same
stage of disease, radiographs of the hands, lower extremities, and spine should be obtained to
evaluate for skeletal dysplasia.2

Epidemiology
The main skeletal dysplasia that mimics LCPD is multiple epiphyseal dysplasia. If
suspected, additional evaluation via genetic analysis is warranted.
LCPD is more common in urban communities than in rural communities.

A predilection appears to exist in certain populations, with an above-average
incidence in Asians, Inuit, and central Europeans. The incidence is below average in
native Australians, Native Americans, Polynesians, and African Americans.
Anatomy and Biomechanics
The osseous and vascular anatomy of the proximal femur evolves through skeletal maturity. The
growing epiphysis is perfused by epiphyseal vessels and is blocked from receiving metaphyseal
vessel contribution by the avascular physis. By skeletal maturity, the physis is resorbed, and the
metaphyseal vessels form anastomoses with the epiphyseal vascularity. This unique progression
allows the proximal femoral epiphysis to remain vulnerable to vascular insult during skeletal
immaturity1,2(Figure 1; Resource 1).
Figure 1 Illustrations show the development of the proximal femur in humans. A, Initially, the
proximal femoral epiphysis in humans consists of avascular cartilage. B, At approximately age 6
months, a secondary ossification center develops because of a vascular system that does not
cross the physis (arrows indicate periphyseal vessels). At skeletal maturity (C), transphyseal
vessels (indicated by the arrow shown crossing the physis) develop, which results in physeal
closure (D). (Reproduced from Leshikar HB, Schoenecker JG: Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease, in
Martus JE, ed: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Pediatrics, ed 5. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2016, pp 269-282.)
Etiology
The exact etiology of LCPD is unknown; most likely it results from a combination of genetic and
environmental factors.

Associated factors
A positive family history is noted in 1.6% to 20% of patients.
LCPD is associated with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder in 33% of patients.
Patients commonly are skeletally immature, with delayed bone age in 89% of patients.

Etiology
Proposed etiologies include mutations in type II collagen, abnormal insulin-like growth
factor-1 action pathways, and various types of thrombophilia. Insufficient blood supply
to the femoral head leading to osteonecrosis is the predominant theory based on the
unique microvascular anatomy of the pediatric proximal femur, the timing of onset of
LCPD, and the relatively tenuous epiphyseal vascularity. Historically, the cause was
thought to be inflammatory or infectious, with transient synovitis as a possible
precursor. Repetitive trauma and exposure to secondhand smoke or carbon monoxide
also are believed to be causative factors. The role of thrombophilia as a cause of LCPD is
controversial. Some studies have reported a 50% to 75% association between LCPD and
a coagulopathy;3-5 other studies have not reported any such association.6,7
Natural History
Waldenström described the initial radiographic observations of LCPD. These stages continue to
be used today8 (Figure 2; Resource 2). Stage I is characterized by sclerosis of the capital femoral
epiphysis. Stage IA is characterized by sclerosis without loss of epiphyseal height, whereas stage
IB begins if loss of height is observed but no fragmentation is present. MRI can be used to
observe early stage I disease before radiographic appearance. Stage II begins if fragmentation of
the capital femoral epiphysis is observed radiographically; stage II is divided into stage IIA and
stage IIB depending on the extent of fragmentation. The extent of involvement of the epiphysis
during fragmentation is the basis of the Herring classification system and guides treatment
recommendations and outcome prognostication. Stage III is characterized by re-ossification
because endochondral revascularization occurs and allows for ossification of the epiphysis. Stage
IIIA and stage IIIB differ in the amount of normal-texture lateral bone re-ossified. The deforming
forces acting on the softened femoral head during stage II cause the femoral head deformation
and resultant asphericity observed in patients with LCPD. Many proposed treatment options

The lateral pillar (Herring) classification of LCPD is based on the height of the lateral 15% to
30% of the epiphysis (ie, the lateral pillar) on an AP view of the pelvis8 (Figure 3).
Group A: no involvement of the lateral pillar with no changes in its density and no loss of its
height
Group B: more than 50% of the height of the lateral pillar maintained
Group C: less than 50% of the height of the lateral pillar maintained
Group B/C border—These groups were later added to the original three-category Herring
classification. In these groups, the lateral pillar is narrow (2 to 3 mm wide) or poorly ossified
or exactly 50% of the lateral pillar height is maintained.
Figure 3 Illustrations show the lateral pillar (Herring) classification of Legg-Calvé-Perthes
disease. Group A hips have no loss of height of the lateral pillar (lateral third of the epiphysis).
Group B hips have less than 50% loss of lateral pillar height. Group C hips have more than 50%
loss of lateral pillar height. In group B/C border hips, the lateral pillar is narrow (2 to 3mm

pillar is maintained without central depression (group B/C 3). (Reproduced from Matheney T:
Legg-Calvé Perthes disease, in Song KM, ed: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Pediatrics, ed 4.

The Catterall classification system defines the extent of involvement of the femoral head in
patients with LCPD (Figure 4). Although commonly used in the past, it recently has been
criticized for its poor interobserver reliability.8
Group I: involvement limited to the anterior head
Group II: anterior and central parts of the head involved
Group III: most of the head involved, with sparing of the posteromedial corner of the
epiphysis
Group IV: entire head involved
Figure 4 Illustration shows the Catterall classification of Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease.
(Reproduced from Matheney TH, Upsani VV: The pediatric hip, in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS

Comprehensive Orthopaedic Review, ed 3. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic

Catterall also described four signs of risk that indicate a more severe course of disease.
The Gage sign (radiolucency in the shape of a V in the lateral portion of the epiphysis)
Calcification lateral to the epiphysis
Lateral subluxation of the femoral head
Horizontal physis
None of the existing classification systems for LCPD are sufficiently prospective to provide a
prognosis before the onset of deformity.

Classification
The advantage of the Herring classification system is that it strongly correlates with
prognosis in patients with LCPD. Its limitation is that the final classification cannot be
determined at the time of initial presentation and that as many as one-third of patients
will be assigned a more severe group as fragmentation stage progresses. An additional
limitation is that the ideal time to intervene is before the fragmentation stage (ie, stage
IIA).
Evaluation/Diagnosis
LCPD is a diagnosis of exclusion.
Other causes of osteonecrosis (eg, septic arthritis, sickle cell anemia, corticosteroid therapy)
and mimicking conditions (eg, skeletal dysplasias, mucopolysaccharidoses) must be ruled out.
Patient History
Clinical presentation
LCPD most often occurs in children aged 4 to 8 years (range, 2 years to late teenage years).
The onset is insidious; children with LCPD commonly present with a limp.
Early in the disease process, many patients have no pain; however, pain in the groin, hip,
thigh, or knee regions typically ensues.

Occasionally, children with LCPD have a history of recent or remote viral illness.

Patient History
A recent multicenter study of 209 patients from 25 centers found that 60% of patients
with LCPD present with pain and a limp, 24% present with pain only, and 15% present
with painless limp.9 Older children (8 years and older) presented with a more severe
limp compared with younger patients. In children who localized their pain, 68% reported
hip pain, 23% reported knee pain, 23% reported groin pain, and 24% reported thigh
pain; many patients presented with multiple regions of pain (Resource 3). Figure 5
shows the presenting symptoms grouped by patient age. Of US patients, 29% were
overweight or obese, 5% had a family history positive for LCPD, 19% were reportedly
exposed to household smoking, 63% reported taking pain medications, and 30% missed
school at least once a month because of pain. The study concluded that more patients
present with pain (84%) than previously reported, some of whom require pain
medications or miss school. This contrasts with earlier studies and historical teaching
that reported a painless limp as the most common presentation.
Figure 5 Bar graph shows presenting symptoms of Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease by age
cohort. (Reproduced from Laine JC, Novotny SA, Tis JE, et al: Demographics and clinical
presentation of early-stage Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease: A prospective, multicenter,
international study. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2021;29[2]:e85-e91.)

Physical Examination
Physical examination may reveal an abnormal gait (antalgic and/or positive Trendelenburg
lurch).
Limitation of hip motion depends on the stage of disease. Range-of-motion (ROM) testing
often reveals decreased abduction and internal rotation. Hip flexion contractures may be
observed in patients with more advanced stages of the disease.
Limb-length discrepancy, if present, is mild and a result of femoral head collapse or disruption
of the proximal femoral physis. Hip contractures may make the limb-length discrepancy seem
greater.

Physical Examination
Early in the disease process, children may present with a limp, minimally restricted
motion, and normal radiographs. The index of suspicion for LCPD should be high, and
follow-up physical examination with repeat imaging studies is indicated.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Plain radiographs
A standard AP view of the pelvis and frog-lateral view of the proximal femur are critical in
making the initial diagnosis and evaluating disease progression.
Early in the disease process, radiographs may appear normal, and early sclerosis may be
extremely subtle. Repeat imaging studies are essential (1 to 3 months later) if initial imaging
studies are negative.
LCPD typically proceeds through four radiographic stages (the modified Waldenström
classification is shown in Figure 2).
Initial Stage
Early radiographic findings are a sclerotic, smaller proximal femur ossific nucleus (because of
failure of the epiphysis to increase in size) and widened medial clear space (distance between

the teardrop and femoral head).
Fragmentation stage (mean duration, 1 year; may be highly variable)
Segmental collapse (resorption) of the capital femoral epiphysis, with increased density of the
epiphysis.
Re-ossification or reparative stage (mean duration, 3 to 5 years)
Begins after necrotic bone is resorbed, with subsequent re-ossification and healing of the
capital femoral epiphysis.
Remodeling stage
Remodeling likely begins while the capital femoral epiphysis is re-ossifying and continues until
skeletal maturity. The amount of remodeling depends on the patient’s skeletal age at the time
of healing.
Computed Tomography
CT has little role in the initial stages of LCPD.

Computed Tomography
The main utility of CT is for three-dimensional evaluation after remodeling at skeletal
maturity to evaluate acetabular coverage and proximal femur morphology. CT may aid in
surgical planning for reconstructive hip preservation surgery, if necessary.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Conventional MRI allows for visualization of the unossified epiphyseal and articular cartilage,
soft-tissue structures, synovitis, extrusion, metaphyseal and physeal changes, and femoral
head shape.

Perfusion MRI (also known as dynamic, gadolinium-enhanced subtraction MRI) often is used to
assess the extent of femoral head necrosis and is a good prognostic imaging modality.
Gadolinium enhancement allows clearer demonstration of the epiphyseal vascularity. Some
surgeons have questioned repeated exposure to intravenous contrast because of concerns for
deposition in the brain and other organs, potentially leading to neurocognitive disorders.
Diffusion-weighted MRI is an imaging technique that does not require contrast. It characterizes
tissues quantitatively via apparent diffusion coefficients. Elevated apparent diffusion
coefficients of the metaphysis show correlation with the lateral pillar (Herring) classification as
early as the initial (sclerotic) phase.
Dynamic MRI more accurately assesses the hip in multiple ROM10 (Resource 4). It has good
correlation with arthrography in the assessment of ROM and hinged abduction.
Bone Scintigraphy
Before the development of MRI, bone scintigraphy was the primary imaging modality to detect
early vascular changes. Limitations of bone scintigraphy include poor anatomic detail and
exposure to ionizing radiation, leading to infrequent use, particularly as MRI technology has
progressed.
Arthrography
Arthrography is useful for assessing coverage and containment of the femoral head in a
dynamic setting.

Arthrography
Dynamic arthrography often is used at the time of surgery to assess the cartilaginous
femoral head shape and extent of coverage by the acetabular labrum. It also may be
used to assess for hinged abduction in hips with substantial loss of motion and
determine the amount of abduction for Petrie cast immobilization that provides
sufficient femoral head containment (Figure 6). Figure 7 shows the difference between
hinged abduction and deformity without hinged abduction.

Three main findings on hip arthrography help delineate a hip with hinged abduction
from a hip with a smooth arc of motion.10
First, as the hip is moved into abduction, the extruded lateral femoral head contacts the
lateral edge of the acetabulum on an AP view, and the extruded lateral portion will not
move under the edge of the acetabulum as the leg is further abducted.
Second, as the leg is brought into abduction, the femoral head center of rotation moves
from the central portion of the head to a position at the lateral edge of the acetabulum.
Third, the medial dye pool increases as the leg is abducted beyond the hinging point,
which indicates that the femoral head is being levered out of the floor of the
acetabulum. This medial dye pooling should not be confused with excess dye collection
superiorly, which may occur in the absence of hinging if the flat portion of the femoral
head moves medially and out of contact with the flat portion of the remodeled
acetabulum.
Pathology
Figure 8 shows the histopathologic changes in a necrotic femoral head over time.

Figure 8 Illustration shows histopathologic changes observed in a necrotic femoral head over
time. (Copyright Texas Scottish Rite Hospital for Children, Dallas, TX.)
Differential Diagnosis
Patients who present with bilateral capital femoral epiphyseal osteonecrosis in similar stages
should be evaluated for skeletal dysplasia. Multiple epiphyseal dysplasia can specifically
present as bilateral LCPD; and additional evaluation via radiographs of the spine, hands, and
knees should be obtained to aid in differentiation. Genetic analysis also should be considered.
Management
Overview
Treatment is based on the patient’s age at disease onset and the severity of involvement of the
femoral head (as defined by the lateral pillar classification).
In general, patients younger than 6 years without complete collapse of the lateral pillar
(group A, group B, and group B/C) can be treated nonsurgically. Most patients achieve
Stulberg grade I or grade II hips at maturity, with 80% achieving a good outcome.
Patients older than 8 years appear to benefit from surgically provided containment of the
femoral head. This is particularly true lateral pillar group B and group B/C border hips.
Patients with lateral pillar group C hips tend to have poor outcomes regardless of treatment
and the age at onset.
For patients aged 6 to 8 years at onset, evidence regarding potential advantages of a specific
surgical procedure in relation to lateral pillar classification is unclear. Femoral- and pelvic-
sided surgical treatment options have been effective in this group. Salvage is performed if
the hip has poor congruency or is no longer containable. The goals of management are to
relieve symptoms and restore stability.
Hinged abduction, in which lateral extrusion of the femoral head results in it impinging on
the edge of the acetabulum with abduction, may be present. Treatment option include the
following:
A valgus-flexion proximal femur osteotomy to place the concentric portion in contact with
the acetabular roof.
Pelvic osteotomy procedures, such as a Chiari osteotomy, shelf arthroplasty, and shelf
acetabuloplasty (labral support procedure), also may be beneficial but have very limited
indications.

For patients with hip pain at skeletal maturity, complex hip reconstructive techniques,
including surgical hip dislocation (SHD) and hip arthroscopy, can be performed to address
residual deformity.

Overview
The management of LCPD is highly controversial. Current treatment options are largely
based on the concept of containing the femoral head in the acetabulum, which
optimizes molding of the soft femoral head and minimizes deformity of the head at re-
ossification. The goal of management is to achieve a spherical femoral head and a
congruent joint to minimize the risk of osteoarthritis. Containment is most crucial during
stages I and II, during which the head is most vulnerable to deformation. Hip pain stems
from synovitis, which leads to motion restriction. This can be relieved by NSAIDs,
protected–weight bearing, and activity modifications. If ROM can be maintained,
continued observation may allow for successful shaping of the femoral head. Limited
motion leads to restricted molding of the femoral head by the acetabulum, leading to
deformation.
For patients aged 6 to 8 years at onset, results are mixed. The results from a prospective
study favors femoral varus osteotomy over physical therapy and the use of a Scottish
Rite orthosis (Resource 5). Another study found no difference between nonsurgical and
surgical treatment in patients aged 6 to 8 years at disease onset11 (Resource 6). Femoral
varus osteotomy performed at the stage of fragmentation had a modest effect on
achieving Stulberg grade I/II hips at 5-year follow-up (43%). A multicenter prospective
study by Wiig et al12 demonstrated better results at 5-year follow-up in patients older
than 6 years with more than 50% head involvement who underwent proximal femur
varus osteotomy compared with nonsurgical treatment (Resource 7).
A 2013 retrospective study suggested a structured approach, via adductor tenotomy
with Petrie cast immobilization followed by A-frame orthoses, can help maintain
containment, which may lead to excellent outcomes, even in lateral pillar group B or
group B/C hips.13 However, earlier multicenter studies did not show a benefit to bracing
if results were pooled with other nonsurgical treatment modalities.14

A 2022 prospective cohort study evaluating patients newly diagnosed with LCPD at 143
of 144 pediatric centers in the United Kingdom identified 371 children (396 hips) over an
18-month period and reported 2-year outcome data on 348 hips (88.5%). Of the 396
hips, 117 (36.4%) were managed surgically. Of the 396 hips, 227 were in the late re-
ossification stage and assigned a Stulberg grade. Predictors of a poorer radiologic
outcome were female sex (odds ratio, 2.27), age older than 6 years (odds ratio, 2.62), and
greater than 50% radiologic collapse observed at enrollment (odds ratio, 2.19). Surgical
management had no effect on radiographic outcomes (odds ratio, 1.03; Resource 8).15
Nonsurgical Management
Containment of the femoral head may be achieved nonsurgically via cast immobilization or
brace management with the hip in an abducted and internally rotated position.
Petrie casts and various abduction orthoses have been used.
Protected–weight bearing also has been recommended, especially during the fragmentation
stage.

Nonsurgical Management
Nonsurgical treatment strategies are most frequently used in patients younger than 6
years at onset, particularly those with lateral pillar group A or group B hips. The
emphasis is on preserving ROM and providing symptom relief. Lateral pillar group A and
B hips tend to be managed in patients of all ages via nonsurgical treatment strategies,
with results similar to those of surgical treatment. Figure 9 shows A-frame cast
immobilization and a subsequent abduction brace strategy used in a patient with
persistent pain and subluxation who was initially treated via shelf acetabuloplasty.

stiffness, and adduction and flexion contractures. The patient previously was treated via

Orthop Surg 2010;18[11]:676-686.)
Surgical Management
Surgical management during fragmentation stages has been shown to result in the greatest
efficacy.
Surgical containment of the femoral head may be approached from the femoral side and/or
the acetabular side based on surgeon preference. These procedures produce comparable
outcomes.
Femoral-sided containment may be achieved via a proximal femur varus osteotomy.
Acetabular-sided containment may be achieved, depending on head reducibility.
Redirectional osteotomy (Salter, triple innominate)
Acetabular augmentation procedure (shelf arthroplasty)
Salvage Chiari osteotomy

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000523

Brace management/cast immobilization and physical therapy may be used to improve
preoperative joint mobility.
Hip arthrodiastasis (via an external fixator) for 4 to 5 months also has been advocated in
some centers but remains controversial.
Multiple epiphyseal drilling has been advocated to stimulate vascular ingrowth into the
epiphysis. This technique is still being studied because it may result in physeal bars, leading
to limited femoral head remodeling and coxa breva.
Surgical management for healed LCPD with residual deformity (Resource 6)
Deformity of the femoral head may result in femoroacetabular impingement (FAI), leading to
secondary pain and loss of function.
Some patients also have structural instability from acetabular dysplasia.
Imaging studies, including radiographs, MRIs, and CT scans, are used to fully assess the
complex three-dimensional deformity.
FAI in patients with LCPD may be managed via SHD and proximal femur osteochondroplasty.
Severe head deformities with preserved extruded lateral femoral head and central head
deformity/necrosis may benefit from a femoral head reduction procedure.

Surgical Management
A review of the results of a prospective multicenter study on the management of LCPD
via femoral osteotomy suggested limiting the varus osteotomy to 15° of correction.12
Additional varus did not reliably remodel and may lead to a Trendelenburg gait with
weakened abductor mechanics because of relative trochanteric positioning.
Redirectional osteotomies typically are performed in hips without hinged abduction on
arthrography. Conceptually, rotating the acetabulum around a nonconcentric femoral
head that hinges will alter acetabular positioning without improving containment and
coverage. In small studies, acetabular augmentation procedures have been reported to
add superior coverage to hips with hinged abduction and have been shown to improve
pain and abduction.16,17
For improved outcomes, the hips must be containable (ie, they must have a relatively full
ROM with congruency between the femoral head and the acetabulum). To allow for

maximal remodeling, the earliest possible initiation of management (before or during

Some patients with Stulberg grade II hips and many patients with Stulberg grade III hips
progress to symptomatic FAI during their teenage years and twenties. This impingement
leads to pain, loss of function, and progressive disability. Some patients also have
structural instability from an associated acetabular dysplasia caused by remodeling of
the acetabulum in response to the deformed femoral head. This manifests as groin pain
with flexion, adduction, and internal rotation of the hip. Limited internal rotation of the
hip is almost universal. Plain radiographs and CT scans aid in the evaluation of complex
structural deformity, and MRIs are used to assess labral and cartilage pathology.
The SHD approach was developed to allow for near-complete dynamic assessment of
the complex deformities leading to multiple intra-articular and extra-articular areas of
FAI. This has led to improved outcomes in the management of this deformity. Patients
with few preoperative arthritic changes who have pain that corresponds with
impingement have the most favorable outcomes.
SHD allows for optimal visualization and correction of proximal femur abnormalities and
residual deformities. Coxa magna can be corrected via extensive resection of the
peripheral femoral head (ie, osteochondroplasty). Femoral head reduction osteotomy
can be performed to remove the central residually deformed portion and allow for the
creation of a more uniform, spherically shaped head. Relative neck lengthening allows
the trochanter to be moved distally along the lateral femur and impinging bone to be
removed from the medial portion of the greater trochanter. This improves the abductor
lever arm and decreases trochanteric impingement on the acetabulum. Labral tears can
be repaired, irreparable labrum can be reconstructed, and cartilage injuries can be
addressed concomitantly.
Secondary instability noted preoperatively or intraoperatively as impingement is
corrected can be addressed via Bernese periacetabular osteotomy. Figure 10 shows the
preoperative and postoperative radiographs of a patient with a complex residual LCPD
deformity corrected via an SHD approach.

Residual deformities
Coxa breva: caused by physeal involvement and subsequent physeal bar, preventing normal
femoral neck growth
Coxa magna—The uncontained, malleable femoral head grows asynchronous to the mold of
acetabulum. This usually is accompanied by a mushroom-shaped femoral head that allows
for a singular plane of motion; however, rotation produces FAI, leading to cartilage and labral
damage.
Overriding greater trochanter: results from normal trochanteric development in patients
with abnormal femoral neck/epiphyseal development; may lead to extra-articular
impingement of the trochanter on the ischium and weakened hip abductor mechanics

correlates with degenerative changes at long-term follow-up18 (Table 1; Resource 9).

The classification system is based on femoral head sphericity and joint congruency at skeletal
maturity.
Grade I and II hips are thought to have a good prognosis because of a spherical and
congruent hip joint.
Grade III, IV, and V hips have a flat head with poor congruence and are thought to result in
hip arthritis.
Many studies combine grades I and II into a single group and compare outcomes with those
of combined groups III, IV, and V.
The risk of premature osteoarthritis of the hip is low (zero to 16%) if the femoral head is
spherical (grades I and II).
The risk of premature osteoarthritis of the hip is high (58% to 78%) if the femoral head is
nonspherical (grades III through V).
Prognosis is related to patient age at disease onset and femoral head deformity at skeletal
maturity. Patients younger than 6 years at disease onset typically have a good outcome. Table
2 lists Stulberg outcome based on chronologic age at LCPD onset and treatment option as
reported by the Perthes Study Group.11
Longer follow-up of patients with LCPD (>45 years) reveals substantial deterioration in hip
function, with only 40% of patients maintaining good function and the remaining 60% of
patients requiring arthroplasty, having severe pain, or having poor function.
Total hip arthroplasty is the primary treatment recommendation for post-LCPD osteoarthritis,
with 96.9% implant survival reported at 15 years19 (Resource 10).
